442.title: An orderly account (Luke 1:1–4)
442.hook: Luke writes to Theophilus, lover of God, so he may know the certainty
442.howItsDone: Catholics hear the Gospel of Luke read through at Sunday Mass every third year (Year C), and Luke's preface is proclaimed on a Sunday in Ordinary Time; his feast day is October 18.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Judas Maccabeus prayed for his fallen soldiers, and fifty days of kings, prophets and wisdom closed. Your line was a holy and wholesome thought. Today, a new block: the Gospel of Luke.

Most books of the Bible never tell you who wrote them, or why. They just begin. Luke is different. Before a single angel appears, there's a preface: four verses that are one long, polished sentence in Greek, the kind that opened histories and medical treatises in that world. The writer steps out from behind the curtain and tells you what he's doing. And he isn't writing to the world in general. He's writing to one person, by name.
screen: `MOST BOOKS JUST BEGIN.` → `FOUR VERSES, ONE GREEK SENTENCE.` → `WRITTEN TO ONE PERSON.`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims: "Forasmuch as many have taken in hand to set forth in order a narration of the things that have been accomplished among us." The first thing he says: others have already tried this. Then where his material came from: those who were eyewitnesses from the beginning, and ministers of the word. Luke doesn't claim to be an eyewitness himself. He's a careful second-generation writer who has, in his words, diligently traced everything from the start. And then: it seemed good to me also "to write to thee in order, most excellent Theophilus, That thou mayest know the verity of those words in which thou hast been instructed." Theophilus is a Greek name: theos, God, and philos, friend or lover. Friend of God. Was he real? Most excellent was a polite title for an official or a person of rank, so he may have been a patron who paid for the copying. But since early centuries readers have noticed that anyone who loves God fits the name, and Saint Ambrose said as much. Both can be true. Theophilus already knows the story; Luke writes so he can stand on solid ground. The Greek for verity is asphaleia: firmness, footing that won't slip. Luke's second volume, the Acts of the Apostles, is addressed to Theophilus too. The Gospel never names its author; early Christian writers name Luke, the companion called the most dear physician in the Letter to the Colossians. For the next fifty days, we read his account in order.
screen: `MANY HAVE TAKEN IN HAND.` · `FROM EYEWITNESSES, NOT AN EYEWITNESS.` · `THEOPHILUS: FRIEND OF GOD.` · `ASPHALEIA: SOLID FOOTING.` · then, large: `THAT THOU MAYEST KNOW THE VERITY.`

segments.voice: Find one thing you're certain of. Not everything, just one thing you could stand on if the floor shook: that someone loves you, that a kindness was real, that God was there in a moment, that truth matters. Let it come, and test it gently: does it hold? If you pray, thank God for that solid ground.
Theophilus. Friend of God, the man Luke addressed his careful, orderly account to, drawing on eyewitnesses from the beginning. Today's word.

443.title: Zachary struck silent (Luke 1:5–25)
443.hook: an old priest doubts the angel and can't speak for nine months
443.howItsDone: Catholics hear the announcement to Zachary at Mass in the days before Christmas and on the vigil of the Nativity of John the Baptist, and some keep silence before the Blessed Sacrament in Eucharistic adoration.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Luke's preface: an orderly account for Theophilus, friend of God. Your line was written for you.

Luke's story doesn't open in Bethlehem. It opens in the Temple in Jerusalem, with an old couple. Zachary is a priest, and his wife Elizabeth comes from a priestly family too. Both, Luke says, were just before God, walking blamelessly. And they had no child, because Elizabeth was barren, and both were well advanced in years. In that world, that was a grief people could see. One day, with his division of priests on duty, the lot falls on Zachary to go into the sanctuary and burn incense. He goes in alone.
screen: `NOT BETHLEHEM: THE TEMPLE.` → `JUST, BLAMELESS, AND CHILDLESS.` → `THE LOT FALLS ON ZACHARY.`

segments.voice: Outside, the crowd is praying at the hour of incense. Inside, Zachary sees an angel standing at the right side of the altar, and he's terrified. In the Douay-Rheims: "Fear not, Zachary, for thy prayer is heard; and thy wife Elizabeth shall bear thee a son, and thou shalt call his name John." Which prayer? Luke doesn't say. Some readers hear the old prayer for a child; others, a priest's prayer for his people. The son will be great, will drink no wine, will be filled with the Holy Ghost, and will go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elias. And Zachary, a good man, standing in the holiest room he'll ever stand in, asks for proof: "Whereby shall I know this? for I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in years." The angel answers: I am Gabriel, who stand before God. Because you didn't believe my words, you'll be mute until the day these things happen. Outside, people wonder why he's taking so long. He comes out and can only make signs, and they realize he's seen a vision. He goes home, and Elizabeth conceives. People often say nine months, but his silence lasts until the baby is born and named. Is it a punishment? The angel says so. But some readers hear something more. A priest whose work was prayers and blessings was given a long season with no words, and when his voice comes back, the first thing it does is bless God. His name, Zachary, means the Lord has remembered.
screen: `THY PRAYER IS HEARD.` · `WHEREBY SHALL I KNOW THIS?` · `I AM GABRIEL. YOU WILL BE MUTE.` · `A SEASON WITH NO WORDS.` · then, large: `FEAR NOT, ZACHARY.`

segments.voice: For a couple of minutes, don't talk, even in your head, as much as you can; when words come, let them pass like people walking by a window. Notice how much of the inner noise is commentary, arguing, planning what to say, and let it quiet down. If you pray, offer the quiet to God and listen.

444.title: Hail, full of grace (Luke 1:26–38)
444.hook: the angel's greeting, Mary's question, and her yes
444.howItsDone: Catholics pray the Hail Mary, whose first half is the angel's greeting and Elizabeth's, in the rosary and the Angelus, and celebrate the Annunciation on March 25; the scene is the first Joyful Mystery of the rosary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zachary asked the angel for proof, and went silent until his son was named. Your line was silence taught him.

Six months later, Luke says, the same angel is sent again. But look where. Last time, the sanctuary of the Temple in Jerusalem, and a priest at the altar of incense. This time, a town in Galilee called Nazareth, and a young woman espoused to a man named Joseph, of the house of David. No altar. No incense. No crowd outside. Luke gives her name last, as if he's saving it: and the virgin's name was Mary.
screen: `THE SAME ANGEL, SENT AGAIN.` → `NOT THE TEMPLE: NAZARETH.` → `AND THE VIRGIN'S NAME WAS MARY.`

segments.voice: The angel comes in and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." Hail, in Latin, is Ave. The Greek word, chaire, was an ordinary greeting that also means rejoice. Full of grace translates one Greek word, kecharitomene, a form meaning something like one who has been graced, and remains so. It's the angel's name for her, almost in place of her name. Catholics hear in it the fullness of grace that marks Mary's whole life; the King James has highly favored. Mary is troubled, and wonders what kind of greeting this is. Fear not, the angel says, you have found grace with God; you'll conceive and bear a son, and call him Jesus. Then Mary asks a question, as Zachary did: "How shall this be done, because I know not man?" But it's a different question. Zachary asked how he could know. Mary asks how it will happen. Some readers notice the difference: one asks for proof, the other for the way. The angel answers: the Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the most High shall overshadow thee. Your kinswoman Elizabeth, the barren one, is in her sixth month, because no word shall be impossible with God. Then her answer: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word." In Latin, fiat: let it be. The angel departs. Catholics keep this moment as the feast of the Annunciation.
screen: `AVE: HAIL, AND REJOICE.` · `KECHARITOMENE: GRACED, AND REMAINING SO.` · `HOW SHALL THIS BE DONE?` · `FIAT: BE IT DONE TO ME.` · then, large: `HAIL, FULL OF GRACE.`

segments.voice: The first half of the Hail Mary is made of Luke's words, with two names added: the angel's greeting, and a few verses on, Elizabeth's. If you pray, say it slowly, one phrase to each breath: Hail Mary, full of grace; the Lord is with thee; blessed art thou among women; and blessed is the fruit of thy womb, Jesus. If you don't pray it, sit with the greeting itself, the Lord is with thee, and notice what it would be like to hear it said to you.
Ave. Latin for hail, the angel Gabriel's first word to Mary at Nazareth, and the first word of the Hail Mary. Today's word.
Your line: full of grace. She asked how, then said yes. That's day four hundred forty-four.

445.title: Zachary's song (Luke 1:57–80)
445.hook: his tongue loosed, he sings of the dayspring from on high, prayed every morning
445.howItsDone: The Benedictus, Zachary's canticle, is prayed every morning at Lauds (Morning Prayer) in the Liturgy of the Hours by priests and religious, and by lay Catholics who pray the Hours.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ave at Nazareth: Mary's question, and her yes. Your line was full of grace.

Elizabeth gives birth to a son, and the neighbors and relatives come to rejoice with her. On the eighth day they gather for his circumcision and naming, and they've already decided: he'll be Zachary, after his father. Elizabeth says no. He shall be called John. But nobody in your family has that name, they say. So they turn to the father, still mute after all these months, and make signs. Zachary asks for a writing tablet. Everyone leans in. He writes four words: "John is his name."
screen: `THE EIGHTH DAY.` → `NOBODY IN YOUR FAMILY IS JOHN.` → `A TABLET, AND FOUR WORDS.`

segments.voice: Immediately, Luke says, his mouth is opened and his tongue loosed, and he speaks, blessing God. The silence ends with obedience: he names the child the way the angel said. And what comes out of him, filled with the Holy Ghost, is a song, called the Benedictus after its first word in Latin. In the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed be the Lord God of Israel; because he hath visited and wrought the redemption of his people." The first half looks back: the house of David, the prophets, the oath God swore to Abraham. Then he turns to the baby: and thou, child, shalt be called the prophet of the Highest, to go before the face of the Lord and prepare his ways. Then the image the carry comes from. The King James says: "the dayspring from on high hath visited us." The Douay says: "the Orient from on high hath visited us: To enlighten them that sit in darkness, and in the shadow of death; to direct our feet into the way of peace." Dayspring and Orient both try to catch one Greek word, anatole: the rising of the sun, the place in the sky where light comes up. Christians hear in it Christ pictured as sunrise, coming to people sitting in the dark. So the Church sets this song at dawn: in the Liturgy of the Hours it's sung every morning at Lauds, Morning Prayer. Months of silence, and the song that broke them became the Church's morning song.

Choose one phrase from the song to meet it, the dayspring from on high, to enlighten them that sit in darkness, or to direct our feet into the way of peace, and say it over slowly until it's yours. If you pray, it becomes a prayer; if not, let it be a way of greeting the light.

446.title: Bethlehem, read slowly (Luke 2:1–20)
446.hook: Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart
446.howItsDone: Catholics hear Luke 2:1–20 at the Christmas Masses at night and at dawn, sing the angels' words in the Gloria at Sunday Mass, and set up a crèche in homes and churches, a custom often traced to Saint Francis.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zachary's song broke his silence: the Benedictus, sung at dawn. Your line was the dayspring from on high.

Plastic figures on a lawn. A school play with a kid in a bathrobe. A stable, an innkeeper, an ox and a donkey, a star. Forget the nativity set for a moment, and read only what Luke actually wrote. It's twenty verses, and it starts not with angels but with an emperor. A decree goes out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be enrolled, and Joseph goes up from Nazareth to Bethlehem, the city of David, with Mary, who is with child.
screen: `FORGET THE NATIVITY SET.` → `TWENTY VERSES, READ SLOWLY.` → `IT STARTS WITH AN EMPEROR.`

segments.voice: Then one sentence, in the Douay-Rheims: "And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him up in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn." That's all. No innkeeper; Luke never mentions one. No ox and donkey; later tradition brought them in from a line in Isaiah, and Saint Francis had a living ox and donkey beside his crib at Greccio. Even inn may be the wrong picture. Luke's Greek word, kataluma, can mean a guest room; it's the word he later uses for the upper room of the Last Supper. So it may have been a crowded family house, with the baby laid where the animals ate. A manger is a feeding trough. And Bethlehem, read as Hebrew, is beit lechem: house of bread. Some Catholic preachers draw a line from there: the child laid in a feeding trough in the house of bread is the one Catholics receive as the bread of life. Then shepherds at night with their flocks, an angel, their fear, and good news of great joy. A multitude sings: "Glory to God in the highest; and on earth peace to men of good will." The Gloria at Mass begins with those words. The shepherds find it just as they were told, and tell everyone, and everyone wonders. Then the quietest line in the chapter: "But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart." Pondering translates symballousa, putting things together, setting pieces side by side. Luke doesn't say she understood it all. She kept it, and turned it over.

segments.voice: Let one thing come up that you haven't figured out yet: something someone said years ago that still comes back, a moment that felt holy and you never told anyone, a hard thing you don't understand. Don't solve it; hold it, turn it over, and set it beside other things you know, the way Mary did. If you pray, ponder it with God.

447.title: Simeon's song (Luke 2:22–40)
447.hook: now thou dost dismiss thy servant, and a sword for Mary's heart
447.howItsDone: The Church sings the Nunc Dimittis every night at Compline (Night Prayer), keeps the Presentation of the Lord on February 2 with the blessing of candles, and counts Simeon's prophecy as the first of Mary's Seven Sorrows.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bethlehem read slowly: no innkeeper, and a manger in the house of bread. Your line was she kept all these things.

Forty days after the birth, Mary and Joseph carry the baby up to the Temple in Jerusalem, to do what the law of Moses asked for a firstborn son and a new mother. Their offering is a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons. That matters: the law allowed birds in place of a lamb for families who couldn't afford one. This is a poor family's offering. And waiting in the Temple courts is an old man named Simeon, just and devout, who had been told by the Holy Ghost that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord's Christ.
screen: `FORTY DAYS, UP TO THE TEMPLE.` → `TWO BIRDS: A POOR FAMILY'S OFFERING.` → `AN OLD MAN, WAITING.`

segments.voice: Simeon takes the child in his arms, blesses God, and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, according to thy word in peace; Because my eyes have seen thy salvation." Dismiss is the key word. The Greek, apolueis, is the word for releasing someone: a servant let go from duty, a watchman relieved at the end of the night shift. Simeon has kept watch his whole life. Now he's holding what he waited for, and he asks to be let go, in peace. A light, he says, to the revelation of the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel. Joseph and Mary are amazed. Then Simeon turns to Mary, and his voice changes. This child is set for the fall and the rising again of many, and for a sign which shall be contradicted. "And thy own soul a sword shall pierce." Catholics count this as the first of the Seven Sorrows of Mary. Then comes Anna, a prophetess, very old, a widow who never left the Temple, fasting and praying night and day. She too gives thanks, and speaks of the child to everyone looking for redemption. Two old people who waited their whole lives, and both recognize a baby. Catholics keep this day on the second of February, called Candlemas because candles are blessed for the light to the Gentiles. And the Church sings Simeon's song every night at Compline, Night Prayer, just before sleep.
screen: `APOLUEIS: A WATCHMAN RELIEVED.` · `A LIGHT TO THE GENTILES.` · `A SWORD SHALL PIERCE.` · `ANNA, WHO NEVER LEFT THE TEMPLE.` · then, large: `NOW THOU DOST DISMISS THY SERVANT.`

segments.voice: Imagine it's tonight and you're about to sleep. Look back over the day, find one thing your eyes saw that was worth seeing, a face, a kindness, a sky, and hold it the way Simeon held the child. Then let the day go, the way a watchman hands over his post; if you pray, you can use Simeon's own words, now thou dost dismiss thy servant.
Nunc Dimittis. Latin for now you dismiss, the first words of Simeon's song when he held the child in the Temple, sung every night at Compline. Today's word.
Your line: in peace. A watchman, relieved at last. Day four hundred forty-seven, in the books.

448.title: He grew (Luke 2:41–52)
448.hook: Jesus advanced in wisdom and age and grace
448.howItsDone: Catholics pray the finding of Jesus in the Temple as the fifth Joyful Mystery of the rosary, and hear this Gospel on the feast of the Holy Family after Christmas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Simeon held the child in the Temple and asked to be let go in peace. Your line was in peace. Today ends the week.

Every parent's nightmare, in five verses. Every year Mary and Joseph go up to Jerusalem for the Passover, and when Jesus is twelve they go as usual. The feast ends. They start home with a company of relatives and neighbors, thinking he's somewhere among them. A whole day's walk later, they look for him. He isn't there. They turn back and search. One day. Two days. Luke says it was after three days that they found him.
screen: `TWELVE YEARS OLD, AT THE PASSOVER.` → `A DAY'S WALK BEFORE THEY NOTICE.` → `THREE DAYS OF SEARCHING.`

segments.voice: He's in the Temple, sitting among the teachers, listening and asking them questions, and everyone is astonished at his understanding and his answers. His parents are astonished too, but not in the same way. Mary speaks first, in the Douay-Rheims: "Son, why hast thou done so to us? behold thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." His answer is the first thing Jesus says in Luke's Gospel: "How is it that you sought me? did you not know, that I must be about my father's business?" The Greek is short and open, literally in the things of my Father: my Father's business, or my Father's house. Translations go both ways. And Luke says plainly: they understood not the word. Then he goes down with them to Nazareth, and is subject to them. The boy who knows who his Father is goes home and does what his parents say. Then Luke's summary: "And Jesus advanced in wisdom, and age, and grace with God and men." The Greek for age, helikia, can also mean stature; the King James says stature, the Douay says age, and both are in it. The Church teaches that the Son of God, being truly human, truly grew, in human knowledge as well as in years. Catholics pray this scene as the fifth Joyful Mystery. After this, Luke says nothing more about him until he's a grown man. That closes the week, and Luke's first two chapters: an orderly account, Zachary's silence, the Ave, the Benedictus, Bethlehem, Simeon, and a boy who grew.
screen: `FOUND AMONG THE TEACHERS.` · `MY FATHER'S BUSINESS, OR HOUSE?` · `HE WENT DOWN, AND WAS SUBJECT TO THEM.` · `HELIKIA: AGE, AND STATURE.` · then, large: `JESUS ADVANCED IN WISDOM, AND AGE, AND GRACE.`

segments.voice: Think back to yourself a year ago, or five, and take Luke's three words one at a time: wisdom, something you understand better now; age, the years and the body that carried you here; grace, a way you've been given more than you earned. Don't grade yourself; just notice the growth, even if it's small, even if it came through something hard. If you pray, thank God for it.
He grew. Luke's words about the boy Jesus after the Temple: he advanced in wisdom, and age, and grace with God and men. Today's word.
